WARSAW (AP) — A Russian plan to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted by Poland before it could be carried out, the Polish prime minister said Thursday, adding it was the first time that “someone on the order of Russia” sought to attack a U.S. citizen on the territory of another NATO country. Western officials have previously warned that Russia stepped up a campaign of targeted killings since President Vladimir Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine , saying they have disrupted several plots across Europe. But Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said this incident was unprecedented. The suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Russia's secret services, was detained by Polish authorities on Aug. 7. He will be held in custody for three months, the Warsaw police said in a statement. The American Ukrainian citizen “was uncomfortable for the Putin regime,” Tusk said in a news conference, without elaborating. The operation was carried out in cooperation with U.S. services, said Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s minister overseeing intelligence services. He said the targeted victim was a U.S. citizen “of Ukrainian origin.” Officials did not immediately provide further details. The Russian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The U.S. State Department said it was aware of the reports but said it had no additional information. Western countries believe Russia seeks to undermine Ukraine's allies Russia has long been accused of targeting its enemies abroad, including by using rare poisons. But intelligence officials previously told The Associated Press that Russia’s security services are now more brazen in their choice of targets, going after Russian activists and foreign supporters of Ukraine as well as military defectors. “We must assume that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons, in various places around the world,” Tusk said on Thursday. He said that Poland and others must be prepared to counter such actions. Western officials see the campaign as connected to Russia’s broader efforts to undermine European countries that support Ukraine . The AP has mapped about 200 acts of sabotage, arson and other disruption across Europe since the start of the war that officials have linked to Russia. President Vladimir Putin told the AP in June that Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. In 2006, British authorities accused Russia of being behind the killing of former FSB officer Alexander Litvinenko in London with radioactive polonium. The U.K. also blames Russia for the attempted killing of former Russian military intelligence officer Sergei Skripal in Salisbury in 2018 with the nerve agent Novichok. German authorities said Russia organized the 2019 killing of Zelimkhan Khangoshvili, a former Chechen rebel commander who was shot in a Berlin park by Vadim Krasikov, a hitman who was later greeted by Putin after he was exchanged in a spy swap . In June, a Russian artist who was critical of Putin was shot and killed at close range near his home in eastern Poland. Tusk said at the time that the killing of Robert Kuzovkov, known by the pseudonym Semyon Skrepetsky, had the hallmarks of a political assassination. He suggested it was possible Russia was behind it but Polish officials have not yet attributed it to Moscow. Last year French officials disrupted a plot which they believe was aimed at killing Vladimir Osechkin, a Russian exile who lives under police protection and works to help military defectors flee Putin’s war. Lithuanian officials also disrupted a plot last year to kill a Lithuanian supporter of Ukraine and another against a Russian activist. Officials in Germany have similarly broken up two plots: one to target the head of a German weapons company supplying Ukraine, the other against a Ukrainian military official . Polish authorities arrested a man in 2024 in what they said was a plot to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . That year, a Russian helicopter pilot who defected was killed in Spain — with Russian operatives the prime suspects. “This campaign is not by accident or chance,” a senior European intelligence official previously told the AP. “There is political authorization.” Burrows reported from London. Stefanie Dazio in Berlin and Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report. https://www.chesterstandard.co.uk/news/2.text: Cheshire Oaks Court Crime Ellesmere Port Sheffield Magistrates Court sentence women for Cheshire Oaks Cheshire Oaks Court Crime Ellesmere Port By Barrie White Chief Reporter Share 0 Comments The trio of thieves were sentenced at Sheffield Magistrates Court. (Image: Google.) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. THREE women who travelled to Cheshire Oaks from Yorkshire to steal thousands of pounds worth of items have been sentenced. Dollaresa Pauce, 28, of Princess Street in Barnsley was joined in the dock at Sheffield Magistrates Court by Estera Stepane, 30, of Hawthorne Street. Both were convicted last July of multiple shop thefts at Cheshire Oaks the previous month with Pauce recording £2,620 of thefts from Calvin Klein, Hugo Boss, Nike and French Connection UK, among others. A total amount of £1,199 was accredited to Stepane who also stole from Doc Martens. A third defendant Raksana Kleina, 24, of Crag View Crescent in Sheffield, was sentenced for her thefts which totalled £759. She was also convicted for driving without a licence and insurance after she took her boyfriend’s car to make the journey to Cheshire Oaks. The bench was told that Pauce had a previous shoplifting offence from 2021. A solicitor for Pauce – originally from Latvia – told the court his client was a single mother with two young children and that ‘there has been no offending since 2021’. He said: “In her pre-sentence report, she admits she shouldn’t have done it and she is working hard to fight the urge of going on the spree she went on. “Since she has been on bail by police, there have not been anything similar to the offending so this allows you to give some sort of community penalty. “But if you are thinking of custody, then could you suspend it or defer it while she makes arrangements for her children. “There is remorse shown in the pre-sentence report and is trying to improve herself by attending church regularly. “She has her family rallying around her to get her back on the rails.” A solicitor for Stepane highlighted her early guilty plea and lack of previous convictions. He said: “She is a carer for her mother and receives payments for that and also has her own mental health issues. “There is genuine remorse because she knows that committing that offence, she has put mother in danger. “She would struggle for unpaid work and also imposing a curfew.” Her solicitor also asked for a potential fine in lieu of a community sentence but also called for a suspended sentence if ‘custody was required’. A representative for Kleina said her client had lost her place on a special needs teaching course and would benefit from mental health support. She said: “She is very remorseful for her conduct and with hindsight, we wouldn’t have made the biggest mistake of her life. “She was on the trajectory of being a special educational needs teacher, but all that has been taken away. “Not only does she lose her good character, she loses that chance at her career. “She said that situation got carried away from her – she has a history of ADHD and while it’s not an excuse, it does affect thinking skills in a heightened state of emotion. “She has been in the UK since the age of two from Latvia and will be attending a university foundation course. “The pre-sentence report is very positive about the background to the offending, and it is that she experienced that adrenaline rush and got caught up in it.” Pauce and Stepane were handed a 12-month community order with 15 rehabilitation activity days, £450 in compensation, £85 and a surcharge of £114. Kleina was given eight penalty points for the driving offences and was also given a 12-month community order including a mental health treatment requirement order, plus costs of £85 and a surcharge of £114. https://www.theblaze.com/lifestyle/intro.text: Michael L. Abramson/Getty Images Introducing News-ique: All the look of real news at a fraction of the value! Josh Slocum October 02, 2026 Outrage bait works because it flatters what we already suspect — and leaves a little Truth-ette behind. Those of a certain age will remember the era of infomercials and QVC. For the younger set, “infomercials” were long-form commercials on cable TV, usually late at night. They ran for five, 10, even 30 minutes, incorporating elements of narrative — usually with laughable skill — to give the feeling that you were watching an actual show rather than a paid advertisement. They hawked products for the home and kitchen with a number to call to place your order. Most of us are just going to click onto the next thing, unaware that the News-ique (TM) item left a Truth-ette (TM) trace in our minds. QVC — “Quality, Value, Convenience” — was/is a TV channel that was nothing but one big infomercial, with on-camera hosts showing off products and bantering with each other and customers who called in. It was online shopping before there was an online. Both marketplaces were famous for offering products that simulated much more valuable items. One such product was the pinnacle: a cubic zirconia stone that was (supposedly) visually indistinguishable from a diamond. It’s got everything: sparkle, allure, and the look of a real diamond at a fraction of the price! Diamonique is forever The best part is the name: Diamonique. Those branding this luxury obviously followed the old drag queen convention for choosing a stage moniker: Take a name denoting quality, seriousness, or at the very least referring to an actual person, then give it a little comic twist that lets you know immediately you're dealing with an imitation. Classic drag queen names of this type include: Hedda Lettuce Virginia Hamm Anita Mann ... to name just a few. As you can see, Diamonique fits right in. So glittering was Diamonique that this imitation spawned imitators of its own, the best of which is Diamelle. When you can’t afford Diamonique, turn to Diamelle! Authentic imitation news What’s amusing in jewelry marketing doesn’t carry over in news and journalism — or what is alleged to be news and journalism. There’s a “news” marketing practice all over social media that gives you what appears to be a news story but is not. I call this News-ique (TM). It has the look and feel of real news but at less than .01% of the value. It’s all over Twitter/X and other social media platforms. The News-ique (TM) formula: Choose a topic guaranteed to rile people whether they’re left, right, or center. The closer the topic is to today’s “discourse” on social media, the better. Write a lede sentence or short paragraph making a claim that flatters the interests, views, but especially the biases of the reader. The text should confirm the reader’s prior assumptions. Include an image that looks very much like it is advertising a published news story, but do NOT include a link to that apparent story. It might or might not be published somewhere, but you can’t know from the original post — that’s the News-ique Difference (TM)! Post nothing else. Do not follow up with a link. Watch outrage flow, and collect clicks and cash. Know your News-ique Here is an example of News-ique (TM), a post on X from an alleged news account, Europa.com . The post includes a picture of the subject against a background that looks “newsy” and “official.” It says this: Poland's Spokeswoman for Children, Monika Horna-Cieślak, used her official powers to take the children of a woman who was rude to her and place them in an orphanage. Horna-Cieślak, 36, who is herself childless, had intervened in a public park in Warsaw before being told by the mother of an unruly child to mind her own business. She then leveraged her authority to have the children seized and placed into care. Why is it News-ique (TM) and not news? Because there’s no link to a fuller source or documentation. There is no follow-up in the thread, only responses from X users. I do not know if this item is real. I have not checked by doing my own search. It does not matter if this particular item is real or not; it is representative of countless posts every day that use the News-ique (TM) formula. My concern is not the content of the story, but the packaging, intent, and effect. News-ique (TM) works because it presents plausible outrages. It’s believable that a head of a government ministry for children’s concerns would abuse her position and target a mother who criticized her. This type of thing happens. We know government officials sometimes abuse their authority and get away with it. Filling in the gaps But what if there is more to this story about a Polish official? What I’m about to write is pure speculation used to demonstrate possibilities. I’m not giving you facts; I don’t even know if the original claim is true. Let’s assume the core of the claim is true. What if the mother did not merely tell the minister to mind her own business? What if she smacked her with her purse? What if she made false and defamatory claims about her online? What if the minister observed that mother abusing her child? The whole story changes if any of those factors are true. If the mother were abusing her child and the minister intervened, then the minister would have been doing the job she is in office for. She looks like a heroine instead of a villain. Again, everything I just wrote was speculation. That’s the point: Without context, detail, and at least some provenance for the original claim, all we are doing is writing fiction while treating that fiction as fact. The political and cultural content cuts in both directions. This example plays to the fears — often real and legitimate — of people with a right-wing bent and to libertarians and other freedom-minded people. But News-ique (TM) items just as often flatter the assumptions of left-leaning people. RELATED: FACTION NEWS: The day the media taught me it’s always wrong to be right H. Armstrong Roberts/Classicstock/Getty Images New pollution The News-ique (TM) approach contributes to political, cultural, and emotional pollution. It leaves an impression of truth in the minds of readers and “consumers.” And no, it doesn’t just work on “stupid people.” It works on most people, smart and stupid, left and right, hysterical or stoic. Items that flatter and confirm our prior assumptions are mentally sticky; they leave a trace you might call Truth-ette (TM). Few are immune. At best, News-ique (TM) is irresponsible and lazy when the content is real and tells a true story. At worst, and I suspect in the majority of cases, it’s a deliberate choice to shade the truth and deprive readers of full context. Outrage gets clicks and cash; sober consideration does not. Some might push back: “You can use Google/Siri/Whatever to check for yourself.” True. But most people won’t. Not even smart people will usually take the time unless they’re going to comment or use it in an essay or podcast. Most of us are just going to click onto the next thing. We won’t necessarily be aware that the News-ique (TM) item left a Truth-ette (TM) trace in our minds. Sometimes, we’ll subconsciously incorporate that item into our view of what’s true about the world. This has happened to me and has probably happened in cases I’m unaware of. When I become aware that I’ve been foolish and failed to check veracity, I admit it in the same thread where I made the claim. Better not to react without having the facts first. Unstoppable There is nothing you or I can do to stop News-ique (TM). There is no way to change the social media incentive structure so this is not a profitable game. The only thing we can do is increase our skepticism and discernment. “Then just stay off social media” is not a workable answer either. Social media is toxic and full of mind games. But it is also the medium through which we can learn many actually true things happening in the world that mainstream news simply will not tell us. Social media is where we can find “citizen journalists” like Nick Shirley who document problems like fraudulent Somali day cares paid for by American taxpayer dollars. When mainstream media gets wind of stories like Shirley’s, it works hard to discredit them, as you see in this CBS News piece. It is also where we can hear directly from politicians and government officials without ABC/NBC/CBS/NPR/NYT leaving out important words to slant the story. We are never going to have a world “back” where “official news” can be relied on. That world never existed anyway; we just didn’t have any way to fact-check the fact-checkers before. If you see a “news story” on Twitter/Instagram/TikTok, make sure you know whether it’s news or News-ique (TM). Check whether context or links are given. If they are, cross-reference the claim against other sources. If they are not, you are reading News-ique (TM). Diamonique can give you sparkle for the soirée at an affordable price. News-ique (TM) is a bad bargain at any price. Want to leave a tip? Josh Slocum is the former head of a nonprofit advocacy group for funeral services consumers. He is the host and creator (along with producer Kevin Hurley) of the "Disaffected" podcast. He also offers consulting and coaching for those dealing with narcissism and family issues. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, has been accused of failing to prepare for power shortage despite clear signs Russia would target the city. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters View image in fullscreen Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, has been accused of failing to prepare for power shortage despite clear signs Russia would target the city. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Kyiv Russian attacks have left Kyiv with devastating power outages – and its mayor in a perilous position As Ukraine’s capital suffers through an energy crisis, many blame Vitali Klitschko for failing to prepare for winter Andrew Roth , Global affairs correspondent Wed 18 Nov 2026 02.00 EST Last modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 09.03 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M aksym Bakhmatov, the outspoken head of one of Kyiv’s largest city districts, did not mince his words when it came to who was responsible for the devastating power outages plaguing his area’s 600,000 residents. “First, because of Putin,” he said from his office in Desnianskyi, a working-class area on Kyiv’s left bank. “Second, because of lack of normal management from the mayor, [Vitali Klitschko]. That’s it.” It may seem unfair to blame a wartime mayor facing daily strikes from Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones for the devastating energy crisis now hitting major Ukrainian cities. Among the worst hit is Kyiv where many homes only have power for four hours a day now, well before the winter months when freezing temperatures will put far more strain on the remaining infrastructure. View image in fullscreen Power outages left Kyiv in darkness after Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure on 8 November 2026. Photograph: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/Getty Images This week Russia struck two crucial bridges in Kyiv crossing the Dnipro river with ballistic missiles, threatening to cut off the two sections of the city – part of a broader strategy aiming to sever the western and eastern sections of the country. But critics argue that the city’s management failed to prepare for the dire power shortages despite clear signs the Kremlin would target Kyiv with strikes that would seek to end its viability as a livable city. Bakhmatov said some homes had already had power outages of up to 37 hours straight. As a district head, he said he did not have the budget or financing to take on the larger projects that he believed should have been implemented over the past five years – decentralising power generation and finding workarounds to help the city survive another winter of Russian attacks. “We have no alternative generators in order to generate electricity inside of Kyiv,” he said. “They didn’t build anything for this, and for now we have almost a collapse of city.” View image in fullscreen Kyiv residents demonstrate outside City Hall demanding Klitschko’s resignation over winter readiness and shelter shortages 17 October 2026. Photograph: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/Getty Images A rare wartime political rally in Kyiv last month gathered about 500 people on the downtown Khreshchatyk street to accuse Klitschko of a number of alleged shortcomings, including the energy crisis. “Kyiv is in blackout – Klitschko will get knocked out,” read one sign at the rally, referring to the mayor’s history as a boxing champion. More concerning than that rally may be the mounting political pressure from Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy , who has blamed Klitschko for failing to prepare for the winter season. “The situation is worst in Kyiv – people and businesses are facing prolonged power and water outages, and the challenges are extremely serious,” Zelenskyy wrote last week in a direct attack on Klitschko’s leadership. “In fact, these are the consequences of the failure to implement decisions at the city level on preparations for the heating season, as well as of this Russian operation against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.” View image in fullscreen Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has attacked Klitschko’s leadership. Photograph: Halil Sağırkaya/Anadolu/Getty Images Klitschko defended himself the same day, asking “How is [Kyiv]… supposed to stop the Russian special operation against the Ukrainian energy system?” The Guardian has previously reported on intercepted Russian plans to make Kyiv uninhabitable , prescribing strikes with specific drones on power plants and substations that could cut off electricity, heating, water, and even sewage systems, causing the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.” Ukraine’s central government is responsible for the defence of most large power plants and other energy infrastructure and the country’s centralised grid means that it is also responsible for trying to keep the lights on and water running in cities around the country. “The mantra of the central government that Kyiv is the worst, its constant manipulations and lies are a bad story,” Klitschko wrote. “Because in its attempts to get rid of Klitschko by any means necessary … the central government is in fact destroying Kyiv.” Volodymyr Fesenko, a veteran political analyst, said the “conflict between Zelenskyy and Klitschko is very old and very personal”. It goes back to when Zelenskyy was a standup comic skewering Ukrainian elites, including Klitschko, and continued after he became president in 2019. The two are not known to have met in person since Zelenskyy became president. View image in fullscreen Musicians plays in a dark underpass in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv during a power outage on 14 November 2026, caused by attacks on energy facilities in the country, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Photograph: Sergei Supinsky/AFP/Getty Images “The city really is not ready as compared with other cities, say, Kharkiv,” Fesenko said, noting the lack of follow-through on promises by the Kyiv government including the construction of more bomb shelters. But the central government also answers for the defence of large infrastructure, including bridges, he added. And then there was Putin, he added, who it appeared had “made a conscious decision to try to break us”. It would be difficult to remove Klitschko as mayor but Zelenskyy’s office had in the past mulled removing Klitschko’s authority over much of the city’s infrastructure, he said. It was not clear if those plans were moving forward at present, and whether Zelenskyy would want to risk further political chaos in an already tense situation. “There is a risk to Klitschko right now. We will see if Zelenskyy ultimately moves forward with efforts to remove him, but it is probably not Ukraine’s biggest political issue right now,” Fesenko said. Demonstrators at the rally last month noted that they didn’t want their protest to be construed as helping Russia undermine the political stability in Ukraine. But the anger at Klitschko was on full display. “We’ve learned in Ukraine that changes usually only come when the fire starts,” said one protester with dyed red hair and a long blue coat, who gave her name as Maryana. When asked what she meant by fire, she answered: “Molotov [cocktails].” Kharkiv, which is about five hours east of Kyiv by car, sits just 19 miles (30km) from the Russian border. In an interview in Kharkiv, the mayor, Ihor Terekhov, said the city faced an even more dire threat than Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities from Russian missiles and cited a “catastrophic” shortage of funding for the efforts to heat the city. “We have set out on a path to decentralise the system that provides utility services, as well as energy services,” he said. That would involve taking Kharkiv off the grid by creating “energy islands” – small, fuel-powered generators that can provide electricity for essential services, as well as modular boilers and other workarounds, he said. “It is very costly and time-consuming.” In Kyiv, Bakhmatov’s office was dark as he spoke. It was adorned with a wall-sized map of his district and plenty of anti-Klitschko posters. He was openly partisan against the current mayor and even said he himself may be a reasonable replacement. But he said he was most interested in representing the people of his district. Its population of 600,000, he said, would make it one of the largest cities in Ukraine on its own, and there was no workable evacuation plan for local residents. They would need to find a way to live out a cold, dark winter there. “We need help with the generators, with food, with power stations, and so on,” he said. “Just help us.” Explore more on these topics Kyiv Ukraine Russia Europe Volodymyr Zelenskyy City mayors features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
